title: Ryschon earns third place at science research competition
text:
Ryschon earns third place at science research competition
S. D. Banks
Ryschon, Sonya Behrends of Alliance, Nebraska, and Danara Abshire of Chadron presented posters at a recent science research conference. The three students are NE-INBRE Scholars who receive financial support, mentorship, and research experience through the program.
NE-INBRE scholars typically participate in a two-year program that includes a 10-week summer research experience at a major research institution in Nebraska and continued research during the academic year. Students receive stipends, housing support, and opportunities to attend national conferences. The program is designed for students in STEM fields interested in pursuing doctoral programs or careers in biomedical research.
Ryschon conducted her research in the laboratory of the University of Nebraska-Lincoln’s Khalimonchuk lab under the mentorship of Dr. Iryna Bohovych, senior research associate. Bohovych said Ryschon worked on a new project linked to the Khalimonchuk lab’s collaboration with Dr. Deepa Dabir at Loyola Marymount University in Los Angeles.
“Using baker’s yeast genetic model, Piper demonstrated that Aim32 protein – a largely uncharacterized mitochondrial protein required for anaerobic growth – plays an important role in mitochondrial copper homeostasis. This finding unraveled Aim32’s functional similarity to human ferredoxin FDX1 – a major regulator of clinically relevant copper-induced cell death,” Bohovych said.
Bohovych praised Ryschon’s approach to research and noted her attention to detail, time management, and work ethic allowed her to generate extensive data. Ryschon also earned a place as co-author on an upcoming manuscript. “She was also strongly encouraged to present her research at the upcoming American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology meeting in Boston next year. It was a true privilege to host Piper in our lab. We are looking forward to hearing about her future successes,” Bohovych said.
Behrends conducted research under Dr. Tim Gatzenmeier at UNL on novel nucleotide anticancer agents. Gatzenmeier said the project focuses on medicines introduced since the 1960s that became cornerstones of chemotherapy but still have unexplored chemical modifications which could address cancer drug resistance.
“Sonya worked with a postdoctoral researcher in my lab and they were able to establish the fundamental synthetic strategy as well as produce several novel agents that are undergoing biological testing,” Gatzenmeier said. “Sonya is a highly talented student with a phenomenal work ethic, and she has a very successful journey in STEM research ahead of her.”
Dr. Shaunda French-Collins, dean of Chadron State College’s School of Business, Mathematics and Science, served as keynote speaker for the gathering.
French-Collins said she hopes INBRE students realize communication is imperative even if they aspire to work primarily in labs or similar settings: “I also hope they realized the importance of often overlooked nonverbal communication such as a handshake, facial expressions, and tone,” French-Collins said. “Students need to be aware of who their audience is while explaining their research...The methodology and results won’t change but how you explain it will.”
